title: Anticipatory vibrotactile cueing facilitates grip force adjustment

findings.consequent: Latency of motor corrective action (grip force adjustment)
findings.mechanism: Baseline reflex action latency to an unexpected load.
findings.quote: The latency of the motor corrective action was 139 ms on average

findings.antecedent: Vibrotactile stimulation (250 Hz or 100 Hz) applied 50 ms before sudden traction load (Conditions 3 & 4) vs. no vibrotactile stimulation (Condition 1)
findings.consequent: Latency of motor corrective action (grip force adjustment)
findings.mechanism: Vibrotactile cues modified reflex reaction, suggesting an anticipatory effect.
findings.quote: when a vibrotactile stimulation was applied 50 ms before the application of the pulling force, the latency was reduced on average to 117 ms.

findings.antecedent: Vibrotactile stimulation only (250 Hz), not cued to respond quickly (Condition 2)
findings.consequent: Latency of conscious response to vibrotactile stimulation
findings.mechanism: Baseline conscious reaction time to an unanticipated vibrotactile cue.
findings.quote: The average latency of the conscious response to the vibrotactile stimuli was 230 ms

findings.antecedent: Vibrotactile stimulation only (250 Hz), cued to respond quickly (Condition 5) vs. not cued (Condition 2)
findings.consequent: Latency of conscious response to vibrotactile stimulation
findings.mechanism: Anticipation of the cue reduces conscious reaction time.
findings.quote: compared to the 229 ±97 ms response... or to the 172±55 ms of reaction time when the cue was anticipated.

findings.antecedent: Vibrotactile stimulation frequency (250 Hz vs 100 Hz) applied 50 ms before sudden traction load (Condition 3 vs Condition 4)
findings.consequent: Latency of motor corrective action (grip force adjustment)
findings.mechanism: Frequency tuning method may not always ensure activation of specific receptor classes.
findings.quote: Finally, we did not find any significant differences between the two frequencies: 250 and 100 Hz.

findings.antecedent: Presence of vibrotactile stimulation (Conditions 3 & 4) vs. absence (Condition 1)
findings.mechanism: No statistically significant effect, though a weak trend of 1-2N increase was observed.
findings.quote: In term of the increases in grip forces, no statistically significant differences were found among conditions.

findings.antecedent: Experimental conditions (loading only, vibrotactile only, load+vibro 250Hz, load+vibro 100Hz)
findings.quote: These values did not significantly vary among the conditions.

findings.mechanism: Initial dynamics dominated by tissue mechanics.
findings.quote: the finger pad deformation started approximately 15 ms later than the onset of the traction force.

findings.consequent: First maximum of finger pad acceleration values
findings.mechanism: Initial dynamics dominated by tissue mechanics.
findings.quote: They reach their first maximums around 30 ms later the onset of the pulling force.

stimuli.description: Instrumented and actuated parallelepiped-shaped handle held between thumb and index finger, capable of being jerked and providing 250 Hz or 100 Hz vibration.

tables.description: Averages and standard deviations of latency, grip increase, and grip handle displacement across different loading and vibrotactile cue conditions.

limitations: It is risky to draw conclusions from apparent correlations between individual grip force increases and finger skin deformations due to high individual variability.
Mechanical responses varied visibly among individuals, suggesting different sensorimotor strategic neural responses to similar inputs.
